As noted above, the central government subdivides its poverty alleviation programs into three distinct clusters. The fi rst cluster is roughly equivalent to SA as defi ned here (but excluding BLT); it accounted for around 63 percent of total poverty alleviation spending in 2010. The second cluster consists of community development and empowerment programs and comprises: (1) Indonesia’s national poverty reduction program (Nasional Pemberdayaan Masyarakat Mandiri, PNPM-Mandiri), which promotes community development and funds rural investment projects; (2) rural infrastructure and empowerment; (3) agribusiness development, and (4) social and economic assistance to isolated and underdeveloped areas. Cluster II has seen a large increase in spending in recent years as PNPM has been scaled up, and most of this spending has been concentrated in rural areas. In 2010, approximately Rp 14,400 billion was spent on Cluster II, equivalent to around 35 percent of total poverty alleviation spending. These programs – often referred to as “community driven development” – take advantage of the political-administrative structure that has been central development in administering most local-level activities since the early 1970s. The system includes the RT (Rukun and PNPM Tetangga), RW (Rukun Warga), and village (Desa/Kelurahan), which are political-administrative units that spatially organize households into consecutively larger self-governing groups. These groups administer social assistance, deliver public goods, and have historically fulfi lled the state’s need for information, control and surveillance. This system, which was fi rst introduced during the Japanese occupation of Indonesia, has historically been strongest, more visible, and judged to be most effective on the island of Java. Examples of the community administrative system in action include delivery of the basic health care for children 5 years of age or less (Posyandu), delivery of family planning services, delivery of basic infrastructure and slum upgrading (Kampung Improvement Program), the Program for Left Behind Villages (Inpres Desa Tertinggal) and more recently Program Nasional Pemberdayaan Masyarakat (PNPM). PNPM, launched in 2006, deserves special attention as it is the operational umbrella for most of Indonesia’s poverty alleviation programs using a community-based approach. PNPM builds on and consolidates the successful experience and structures of three community-based poverty alleviation programs: (1) the Kecamatan Development Program (KDP), (2) the Urban Poverty Program (UPP), and (3) the Program for Left Behind Villages (IDT). PNPM‘s overarching objective is to alleviate poverty through both improved socioeconomic conditions, including more and higher quality public goods, and improved community-level governance. PNPM provides grants directly to community- level organizations; these organizations essentially apply for those grants by hosting collaborative and consultative meetings where members discuss and decide on a proposal for the use of the block grant monies. PNPM grants reach every sub-district in Indonesia every year, and a competitive process allocates the grants to community groups with the best proposals. In urban areas, PNPM block grants facilitate the achievement of a collaborative community development plan. Communities also benefi t from support for activities jointly proposed by the government and funded on a cost-sharing basis. The main poverty alleviation activities that urban areas have so far chosen to use PNPM funds for include: infrastructure projects, increased poverty awareness through social mapping at the community level, elections for community organizations, women’s empowerment through increased participation in community governance and access to revolving credit, and disaster recovery in the form of housing reconstruction.

In rural areas PNPM delivers two types of block grants. The fi rst funds village investment proposals (as in urban areas) and the second supports the participatory planning process it self. Besides a limited list of prohibited activities, investment opportunities for communities are open. Villages can also participate in a number of special pilot programs. These include responses to natural disasters, community-based post-confl ict reintegration, conditional cash transfers to improve health and education outcomes, natural resource management and renewable energy initiatives, technical assistance and fi nancial resources for poor farmers, and other pilots that focus on remote geographic areas and cultivating localized approaches to poverty alleviation. Indonesia has an impressive record at successfully reducing poverty through community- based programs. The achievements in poverty reduction through public expenditure in this area are well documented.4 Some of the most robust evidence comes from recent impact evaluations of PNPM.5 The Cluster II community development approach has the potential to address manifestations and correlates of household or individual poverty that are related to access to, or the quantity and quality of, local public goods and locally-produced entitlements (like health and education services) as well as issues that have to do with community organization and voice and links to local government. Social insurance expenditures, which mainly fund servant pensions, have also increased and still exceed SA expenditures although far fewer families and individuals are covered by centrally-funded insurance programs. In 2004, the central government passed the National Social Security System Act which included the promise of universal social coverage for all Indonesia. This system has not yet been implemented, but public expenditures on social insurance are still growing quickly in real terms and exceed SA expenditures. In 2010, the central government spent an estimated Rp 54,326 billion on social insurance, equivalent to 7.7 percent of total central government expenditures and 0.8 percent of GDP. Indonesia Social Assistance Program and Public Expenditure Reviews are policy notes summarizing current issues in the Government of Indonesia’s major household-targeted social assistance programs. Design, implementation, coverage, impacts, budgetary demands, cost effectiveness, stakeholder perceptions, and program history will be examined through qualitative and quantitative analysis for each program: conditional and unconditional cash transfers, subsidized rice distribution, a health fee waiver, cash scholarships, and cash transfers for the neglected elderly, disabled, and at-risk youth. Evidence-based appraisal can assist policymakers in evaluating programs and deciding whether and how they are achieving Indonesia’s social protection goals. Reviews 1 through 8 together comprise a companion volume to the “Protecting Poor and Vulnerable Households in Indonesia” report. “Protecting Poor and Vulnerable Households in Indonesia” provides a public expenditure review of the wider social assistance sector, summarizes results from Reviews 1 through 8, explores gaps in both population coverage and risk coverage of current social assistance programming, and offers recommendations and suggested reforms for achieving an integrated and coordinated household-based social assistance system. Bulgaria is facing a dual challenge in the next few years: the first one is to raise employment and productivity to narrow the income gap and facilitate the convergence with the EU. The second one is to program the forthcoming EU grant funds in a manner that promotes income convergence and ensures continued macroeconomic stability. To facilitate income convergence with the EU, efforts to increase employment and productivity are particularly pressing for Bulgaria, because the country has a declining working age population. At the same time, the country has the second lowest labor market participation and the lowest employment rate among Central and Eastern European (CEE) countries, with a large share of employment in unproductive segments of the economy, or in areas where labor productivity is stagnant. The forthcoming EU structural funds, which are designed to help Bulgaria achieve income convergence, provide an unprecedented opportunity for the country to catch up with the EU standards of living, ifu sed wisely. However, given the magnitude of expected resource flows, using them wisely is also a challenge. 2. This report explores the options available for the Bulgarian government to use optimally both the EU grant and Bulgaria’s own funds in the pursuit of enhanced economic growth and development. The analysis has selectively focused on four areas-nhancing the skills oft he labor force; agriculture; roads; and environmental protection. These areas were selected because they will either receive the bulk of expected EU funds or if used wisely, are most likely maximize the longer term positive impact on productivity and growth. In each area, the report has explored the priorities for funding, and implications of the forthcoming resource flows. In addition, estimates of EU transfers in the first three years of accession have been prepared, both in terms of net transfers to the country (net impact on the balance payments), and the magnitude of funds expected to flow annually through the government budget. I. FINANCIALA ND BUDGETARIMY PACT OF PROJECTED EU FUNDS: 3. The net overalljinancial effect of expected EU grant funds is projected to be highly positive on Bulgaria, about 3.7 percent of annual GDP on average during 2007-2009, if the country takes all available funds. Experience from EU15 countries indicates that, if effectively used, the EU funds can contribute to economic growth both in the short and long run. In the short run they would create increased domestic demand. In the long term, ifi nvested in the improvement of the physical and human capital with high economic returns, they have the potential of making an important contribution to economic growth through the supply side. However, experience also shows that, if badly used, these resources may have only a short-term positive demand effect on the economy, and in the long term lead to real appreciation of the local currency and reduced competitiveness, aid dependency, and undermine the efforts to improve governance. Funds have proven to be most effective, when put to use under broad and well-defined strategic programs. 4. Beyond the net overall financial effect, the report shows that Bulgaria’s fiscal position would deteriorate by about two percent of GDP on average during 2007-2009, if the government absorbed all the available funds and there was no restructuring of the fiscal framework. The analysis indicates that the deterioration of the national budget balance would stem from increased expenditures. Taking into account the already high level of public spending, it would be essential to improve the ability of the government to substitute existing expenditures with EU funds--that is, to reorganize the budget in the most efficient way to maximize the absorption of EU funds. The need for restructuring is even more acute in the light of expanding social spending, related to the rapidly aging population, and high unemployment. 5. The analysis suggests that there is potentially ample room in the Bulgarian budget to absorb the expected sharp increase in transfers from the EU by consolidating and increasing efficiency of existing expenditures, without adversely affecting economic growth. Since the government would like to cap the level ofp ublic expenditures as a share of GDP at 40 percent, adding EU funds to the budget without any expenditure restructuring is not an option. That leaves the government essentially with two choices in terms of accommodating the expected EU funds. The first choice is to accommodate them through full fiscal adjustment: through fiscal consolidation equivalent to the projected budgetary impact of EU funds-that is, about two percentage point of GDP. The numbers suggest that the first choice could be achieved solely by rationalizing spending on military, security, health, government employment, subsidies, and social benefits. The second choice is to accommodate the EU funds through a mixture of fiscal adjustment and economic growth. However, from the point of view

A mentioned earlier, a large share oft he forthcoming EU grant funds is expected to go to support education initiatives, upgrading of roads, implementation of the European common apcultural policy, and environmental standards. In each of these areas, the report analyzed options for utilization of EU funds. 7. Education: There is an urgent need to modernize the Bulgarian education system to ensure the country has a highly skilled and productive labor force that can make the catching up with the EU standards ofl iving a reality. This is critical since while the level of education is steadily increasing in EU countries, the participation rate in higher education has been declining Bulgaria. The demographic change and declining age cohorts provide an opportunity to improve the efficiency of public education spending, and ensure it is spent effectively on improving the quality of education and training and increase coverage oft he shrinking age cohorts of students. 8. The report recommends that the government does not increase public spending on education as a share of GDP, but seeks efficiency gains within the existing resource envelope. This is advisable, since public spending on education, when adjusted for income per capita, is already on a level comparable to many CEE countries, and spending per student has been steadily increasing, but education outcomes remain well below CEE levels. Provided credible reform is taken, maintaining the existing level ofp ublic spending on education as a share of GDP (including possible EU funds) would be warranted. While consolidation of spending is recommended in many other sectors, given the importance of education for promotion ofl abor productivity, a differential treatment is recommended on education, assuming reforms proceed. Reform of the education system would also build a good base for a more productive use of EU grant funds, and make human resource development programs presented to the EU for funding more credible. 9. The reform measures needed would include gradual consolidation of schools, universities, and vocational colleges in light of declining age cohorts to increase student-teacher ratios and release funds for upgrading of curriculum, textbooks, and facilities. Reforms need to be guided by a leadership group that consults regularly, including across ministries (MES, MLSP, MEE), and that unifies the vision across ministries with periodic Position Papers that set out not only the vision, but progress to date and the way forward. Explaining the potential benefits of such reforms is crucial for successful implementation. Producers of dairy would also suffer an initial small loss of income, as would some medium to large-size farmers (50-100 hectares) due to crop-specific effects rather than size effects. The latter, however, would only be a short-term impact, and turn into income increases in the first year after accession. It, therefore, does not justify top-ups. Topping up is expensive, competes with other more productive programs, and establishes a sense of entitlement which makes it politically difficult to remove it later. Given the arguments in this report on keeping the size oft he state in check and on focusing all new expenditures on improving productivity, topping-up is not the way forward. A different mechanism of support should be sought ifi t is necessary for political reasons, perhaps best done through the financing potentially available under Pillar 2. 14. Payment Modalities: If nevertheless topping-up is chosen, evidence suggests that the application of specific, coupled CNDPs to limited sub-sectors (tobacco) should be favored over the implementation of broad, sector-spanning top-ups. Moreover, such support should have a sunset clause. Also, since support to specific products introduces distortions into production patterns, the form of CNDPs chosen ... should be as simple as possible. Support to particular regions or sub-sectors would best be addressed under Pillar 2 as part of general rural development of a specific region. This would also fit better into strategic considerations ofi nternal convergence among Bulgaria’s regions, and with the expected strategy for rural development in the EU in general. 15. Eligibility Criteria: According to EU rules, the minimum parcel size for which payments may be requested under SAPS is 0.3 ha, and the minimum holding size eligible for support under SAPS is 1. O ha. Bulgaria can decide to set the minimum size of eligible area per holding at a level higher than 0.3 ha, as long as it does not exceed one hectare. Fixing the eligibility threshold at the 1.0 hectare level would exclude about 76 percent of all farms, but only 6.6 percent of agricultural land in Bulgaria. Some preference was noted in the Ministry of Agriculture for a mixed threshold model of 0.3 ha for intensive farming and one ha for all others. This is possible, although this report has argued for a single eligibility criterion ofo ne hectare. In making this decisions the authorities will have to weigh carefully the benefits of structural change that would be promoted through consolidation of farms into larger more efficient units, and the reduction of costs stemming from not having to administer the SAPS for very small farms versus the adjustment costs for the farmers that would retire. 16. Transfers among Budgetary Allocations: If Bulgaria decides to top up, there are two ways to do it. It can top up the direct payments coming from the EU from its own resources, or it can top them up by using up to 20 percent oft he monies available under Pillar 2, but it must provide counterpart-financing of these diversions from Pillar 2 funding from its own resources. The Pillar 2 route is obviously fiscally less demanding, but it would take funds away from activities that potentially have a much larger impact on the competitiveness ofB ulgaria’s agnculture than direct payments to farmers. 17. Efficiency Considerations: Direct payment schemes such as SAPS can provide some level of income stability, and help mitigate farmers’ exposure to income risk by guaranteeing a minimum income from farming. Direct support schemes, however, cannot substitute for the need to raise the productivity and improve the competitiveness of Bulgarian agriculture. Productivity growth and improved competitiveness remain the only sustainable solution to agricultural income problems. Agricultural support schemes targeting specific sectoral adjustment needs, such as farm consolidation, productivity or competitiveness-enhancing farm-level investments, and diversification to off-farm activities is the way forward. These can be tailored to the specific needs oft he different regions, and it can all be done under Pillar 2. 18. In addition, direct income support payments may reduce the incentives for farmers to restructure, consolidate, and modernize. Direct income payments may reduce incentives for consolidation, because they guarantee a minimum income from farming, and therefore reduce the incentive for unprofitable or older farmers to sell or lease their assets to more productive entrepreneurs. SAPS payments and their effects on land prices or land rental rates may also make land consolidation more difficult, in particular in a farming environment in which agricultural credit is not well developed. Evidence from EU member states indicates that support payments granted on a per hectare basis lead to significant increases in prices for buying and especially leasing agricultural land. This will significantly disfavor tenants, slow the consolidation toward more viable farm sizes, and would in effect support land owners rather than farmers. These trade-offs between direct income support payments, and the need for higher productivity and competitiveness point to the need to clearly separate rural social measures (such as measures to reduce social tensions and provide social protection in the rural areas) from the major instruments ofa gricultural income support. 19. BULGARIA’S EU ACCESSION AND AVAILABILITY OF EU FINANCING 1.1 Bulgaria is close to joining the European Union. With accession there could be a potentially large net transfer of grant resources from the EU to Bulgaria. The aim of these transfers will be to facilitate Bulgaria’s income convergence with the rest of the EU. Given the much lower standard of living in Bulgaria, the EU has committed a considerable amount of assistance to the country after its expected accession in 2007.’ In 2004, the EU committed EUR 4.6 billion in 2004 prices to Bulgaria for the period 2007-2009. Since then the figure has been increased to reflect increased funding for rural development. 1.2 It is an opportunity that does not come along too often for a country. Hence, it is natural that the Bulgarian government is focusing on how to optimize the use of the projected grant transfers from the EU. The government wishes to do that in the context of optimizing all its public expenditures, since, while the EU grant funds themselves may well be optimally used, they may provide room for other expenditures from Bulgaria’s own resources to be allocated sub-optimally. Hence, the problem is one of optimizing the entire public expenditure envelope, regardless oft he source oft he funds. 1.3 The opportunity of extra funds from the EU comes with a huge challenge: namely, to ensure that the EU grant funds together with own funds are used in a manner that helped Bulgaria converge to the EU standard of living. At roughly 30 percent of the average GDP per capita for EU25 (in PPP terms), Bulgaria’s starting position is not enviable. It also faces a demographic challenge. Bulgaria’s population is declining at almost one percent per year, its labor participation rate of 5 1 percent and its employment rate of 46 percent are among the lowest in Europe,’ and the productivity of its labor force is low. Analysis in the recent Country Economic Memorandum on Bulgaria (World Bank 2005) shows that assuming a rise of its participation rate from 50 to 70 percent by 2015 and that

employment rate of 46 percent are among the lowest in Europe,’ and the productivity of its labor force is low. Analysis in the recent Country Economic Memorandum on Bulgaria (World Bank 2005) shows that assuming a rise of its participation rate from 50 to 70 percent by 2015 and that GDP per capita can be made to grow at 5.5 percent per year for the next twenty years, Bulgaria will reach two thirds oft he EU25 average GDP by 2025. The problem is that while there are many countries that manage to grow at those rates for a decade, the number that achieves that for two consecutive decades drops off precipitously, and three decades ofs uch rapid growth in a row is a rare event. In the face of such odds, errors will be costly. Hence the huge challenge. 1.4 The magnitude of the remaining challenge may well sound as a discouraging message after Bulgaria has done so well in the past few years. As Table 1.1 shows, GDP growth has been in the 4-5 percent per year range for the past 7 years. Its pace has moved into the 5-6 percent range in 2004, and seems to have kept up so far during 2005. The unemployment rate has been falling, and as ofN ovember 2005 was approaching ten percent, although this should be tempered by the realization that this is in the context of very low labor participation and employment rates. Private investment has been growing strongly, in part driven by foreign direct investment. The budget is in balance, the underlying structural budget is also in a good shape, primary budget is strongly positive, reserves are strong, and public debt has fallen precipitously relative to GDP and is now well within the Maastricht bounds. As a result, Bulgaria’s sovereign debt ratings have strengthened to investment grade. Perhaps the one dark cloud on the immediate horizon is the current account deficit, which is currently running at over 14 percent ofG DP on an annual basis. This could present a problem, if foreign direct investment inflows were to slow down sharply. For this reason the authorities need to continue to be vigilant to protect the growth momentum that has been achieved through prudent fiscal policy. ’ Assuming Bulgaria joins the EU in 2007, as is currently planned. OBJECTIVE OF THE REPORT 1.6 This report aims to assist the Bulgarian government in exploring their options for the optimal use of both expected EU grants and Bulgaria’s own funds in the pursuit of enhanced economic growth and development. The analysis focuses on the EU commitments to Bulgaria in the first three years of accession, estimates the projected net EU grant flows to the country and the budget, and highlights options to accommodate them into the budget (Chapters 1-2). In addition, the report explores the priorities for funding, and implications of the forthcoming resource flows in four areasdnhancing the skills oft he labor force; agriculture; roads; and environmental protection (Chapter 3-6). These areas were selected because they will either receive the bulk of forthcoming EU funds or, if used wisely, are most likely to maximize the longer term positive impact on productivity growth. 11. Transfers from these funds will need to be channeled in a way that facilitates three Cs - convergence (both external and internal), regional competitiveness and employment, and European territorial cooperation. POLICIES FOR GROWTH AND FISCAL SUSTAINABILITY 2.1 The government has three choices to accommodate the expected EU grant funds. The first one would be to add the funds to the budget without any fiscal adjustment, and let public expenditures increase as a share ofG DP. This would initially worsen the budget balance. The second option would be to accommodate them through full fiscal adjustment equivalent to the projected budgetary impact of EU funds-that is, about two percentage points of GDP. The third option would be to accommodate the EU funds over time through a mixture of fiscal adjustment and economic growth. 2.2 Of these options, accommodating the expected EU funds to the budget through full fiscal adjustment would be recommended both from the point ofv iew of increasing growth in the long run and to make space for, say, further reductions in payroll taxes. The first option is ruled out, since the Bulgarian government has expressed a clear intent to keep their public expenditures at their current level of4 0 percent of GDP or below. Following the third option would be risky, since GDP growth cannot be controlled by the government, and budget plans should be made on the basis of prudent assumptions about revenue growth. 2.3 This chapter explores the fiscal challenge presented by the second option: whether full fiscal adjustment would be feasible. It also begins to explore options to make space in the national budget for the expected EU funds. The chapter, after presenting the main outlines of Bulgaria’s national budget (by sector/function), goes on to analyze what the appropriate size ofB ulgaria’s government might be given its level of development, and where the savings to reduce the size ofg overnment might be found. HOW LARGAE G OVERNMENT? 2.6 When viewed through the lens of “dependency” ratios mentioned in Chapter 1--each employee in the formal private sector supporting at least three other Bulgarians--it becomes clear why the public sector needs to be made more efficient and probably smaller relative to GDP than it is now. A restrained public sector would reduce the burden on the private sector and thus help make it stronger. At the moment, public expenditures in Bulgaria are about 40 percent of GDP. It is a level that the Bulgarian authorities would like to sustain and preferably reduce, while keeping the budget in balance. This would allow them to retain some fiscal flexibility in the face ofp otential negative shocks, the most threatening of which in the short run may well come from the side of the current account, although pressures from politically powerful sectors for increased expenditures could also play their part. 2.7 Public spending at 40 percent of GDP implies a heavy tax burden on households and private business, as high taxes and contributions are practically unavoidable at such a spending level. This is a concern because high taxes generally distort economic incentives and transfer resources from the private sector to the public sector, which is typically less efficient, and thereby reduce the growth potential of a country.’ While some studies of relatively advanced economies have found no impact of taxation on growth, most find a negative effect and no study has shown positive growth effects ofh igh taxation.* 2.8 Not all taxes have equally distortionary effects, however. High marginal tax rates on income and profit are more distortionary than proportional taxes on consumption such as the value-added tax. For this reason tax reforms often aim to increase economic efficiency by broadening the tax base, while lowering marginal rates on consumption and saving, or by replacing income taxes with proportional sales taxes. CONCLUSION 2.33 This section has tried to establish that there is ample room for Bulgaria to reduce the size of its government, and thus accommodate the likely level of EU transfers that will come after the expected accession without having to reduce growth. Bulgaria’s public expenditures in the aggregate seem to be between 3 and 8 percent of GDP higher than would be necessary to keep pace with the growth of a sample of rapidly growing countries, while improving

EU transfers that will come after the expected accession without having to reduce growth. Bulgaria’s public expenditures in the aggregate seem to be between 3 and 8 percent of GDP higher than would be necessary to keep pace with the growth of a sample of rapidly growing countries, while improving many of the outcomes. The fact that the private sector is still weak and is carrying a large tax burden also argues for a smaller state. Finally, an examination ofp ublic expenditures in terms off unctional and economic classifications suggests that there should be room for expenditure reductions relative to GDP in health, social benefits, and size oft he civil service, defense, and security. The envelope for education may be about right at the moment, but like in other sectors, there is a need for pressing on with the reforms to improve outcomes. As will be argued in the next chapter, reforms in education, because of its relevance to long-term rapid growth, are crucial to the successful (growth-promoting) absorption oft he EU funds. 2.34 Reductions will take political resolve. Change means losses for some of the vested interests, so there is bound to be resistance. The challenge is to be able to convince people that a large majority will gain from well designed changes. Bulgaria’s government has gone through difficult changes in the past 15 years and in the past few years has finally seen some fruits of these efforts. It would be important not to lose the unique opportunity of substantial grants from the EU to help it weather further reforms. This chapter suggested some areas where greater efficiency in the use off unds could help Bulgaria maintain its momentum. It is crucial that the same discipline that has been suggested for the various categories of expenditure also be applied to the funds that will be coming from the EU. The areas that are likely to receive the most funds are agriculture, transport, human resource development, and environment. For this reason the remaining chapters (Chapters 3-6) of this report focus on how the expenditures in these areas could best be targeted on programs that would help raise productivity and sustain the convergence of Bulgaria’s GDP per capita to that ofE U25. 3. The education is proposed to be made results-oriented; by linking funding to the quality of the education product. Education delivery is to be decentralized and autonomy given to schools, while the school network is proposed to be optimized. Above all, conditions for real and profitable student learning as well as for lifelong learning are to be created by establishing linkages between the educational establishment and business. 3.15 These policy objectives and priorities are in line with EU policy concerns. Traditionally, the EU policy on education has been tentative and cautious, the prerogatives on education being left very much to the member states. In recent years, and particularly since the Lisbon Objectives of 2000, while still respecting the rights ofm ember states, the EU has adopted a strong stance on education policy. It regards education and training as central to making Europe “the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world capable of sustainable economic growth with more and better jobs and greater social cohesion.” In 2004 the European Commission stated: “The European Social Fund will also support actions to expand and improve investment in human capital, in particular by improving education and training systems, and action aimed at developing institutional capacity and the efficiency of public administrations at national, regional and local level” (European Commission, 2004). 3.16 However, as highlighted above, the record of education policy implementation in Bulgaria is not an impressive one, and hence it would be important to ensure that the current plans are effectively implemented. THEO PPORTUNITY PROVIDED BY EU ACCESSION. 3.17 The forthcoming EU accession provides an unprecedented and historical opportunity to move the planned reforms forward, by providing incentives and leverage for change as well as external funding. The government would need to take the advantage of the period prior to accession to prepare for and launch the planned major educational reforms. 3.18 In preparation for reform, five steps would need to be taken: 3.19 First, a communications and public relations campaign would need to be initiated to inform the government staff and the public of the purposes, and advantages to be gained from the reforms. The advantages and changes to teachers, school leaders, VET personnel, and higher education personnel would need to be clearly spelled out. The role and benefits of EU Structural and Regional Funds would need to be explained to people who are often removed from policy planning and negotiations, and the historical window ofo pportunity would need to be highlighted. 3.20 Second, the core principle which ought to drive the process of change is the centrality of human resource development-education and training--for a modem knowledge-based economy. It is essential that education and training reforms have a high priority on the government agenda. The responsibilities of the Ministry of Education and Science (MES) and the Ministry of Labor and Social Policy (MLSP) converge on a number of areas of human resource development. Therefore, since the successful implementation ofr eforms requires an inter-ministerial effort, it would be ofu tmost importance that these ministries collaborate and closely coordinate the reforms for the common good. 3.21 Third, MES should also consider establishing a Strategic Policy Unit to focus on policy and strategy implementation, and devolving routine activities to other units. MES, which together with MLSP I has a crucial role to play in driving the reforms, is compartmentalized and fragmented, and there is inadequate communication between sectors within the ministry. As a result of this, the big picture, into which the components fit, tends to get lost. The top management team of MES should also meet on a regular basis on policy matters to ensure consistency, cohesiveness and lack of contradiction in what emerges. 3.22 Fourth, to ensure all staff is aware ofo ngoing activities and reforms, MES would need to prepare and regularly update a position paper summarizing all the education and training initiatives underway, indicating the timetable for their development and implementation. CONCLUSIONS 3.62 There is an urgent need to modernize the Bulgarian education system to ensure the country has a highly skilled and productive labor force that can make the catching up with the EU standards ofl iving a reality. This is critical since while the level of education is steadily increasing in EU countries, participation in higher education and education outcomes have been declining Bulgaria. 3.63 The forthcoming EU accession provides an unprecedented opportunity for the Bulgarian government to move the planned education reforms forward, by providing incentives and leverage for change as well as external finding. At the same time, the demographic change and declining age cohorts provide an opportunity to improve the efficiency of public education spending, and ensure it is spent effectively on improving the quality of education and training of reduced numbers of students. The government would need to take advantage oft he period prior to accession to make this happen. 3.64 The government would be well-advised not to increase public spending on education as a share of GDP, but rather to seek efficiency gains within the existing resource envelope. This is important, since public spending on education is already on a level comparable to many CEE countries, and spending per student has been steadily increasing, yet education outcomes remain well below CEE levels. Provided credible reform is taken, maintaining the existing level of public spending on education as a share of GDP, including possible EU funds, would be warranted.*' While consolidation of spending is recommended in many other sectors (see chapter 2), given the importance of

education outcomes remain well below CEE levels. The savings from school consolidation should be retained within the sector, and used to finance quality improvements. To raise the quality of education, there is a need to undertake a curriculum reform, develop better teaching materials, improve teacher training, open University administration to outside representatives, and establish periodic national student assessments to evaluate the impact of education. At the upper secondary and university levels, it is critical to establish links with the labor markets to ensure students are equipped with skills required in the market. In a global economy, continuous upgrading of labor skills is increasingly important to stay competitive, and hence would need to be encouraged. Further engaging the private sector in education delivery could also be very important. 3.66 The proposals for projects presented in this chapter for possible EU funding, even though, tilted towards the interface between the education system and the market, form a broad education and human development reform package consistent with the EU education policy. The concerns underpinning the proposals relate to key policy concerns of the Bulgarian authorities, such as: (i)im proving the quality of education; (ii)m odernizing the educational infi-astructure; (iii)i mproving access for all; (iv) reducing inequalities; (v) promoting social inclusion; (vi) building the capacity of personnel; and (vii) promoting lifelong learning. 3.67 With careful planning and strong leadership Bulgaria can achieve its human resource development goals. The potential is there, but it will not be realized without a great deal of effort. This would suggest that no top-ups are required to maintain and increase average producer incomes. However, the impact would be uneven across the producers of various agricultural products. Income from tobacco production would even decline as current direct payments are replaced with those under CAP. Producers of dairy would also suffer an initial small loss of income, as would some medium to large-size farmers (50-100 hectares) due to crop-specific effects rather than size effects. The latter, however, would only be a short-term impact, and turn into income increases in the first year after accession. It, therefore, does not justify top-ups. Topping up is expensive, competes with other more productive programs, and establishes a sense of entitlement which makes it politically difficult to remove it later. Given the arguments in this report on keeping the size of the state in check and on focusing all new expenditures on improving productivity, topping-up is not the way forward. A different mechanism of support should be sought if it is necessary for political reasons, perhaps best done through the financing potentially available under Pillar 2. 4.50 Payment Modalities: If, nevertheless, topping-up is chosen, simulations carried out for this report suggest that the application of a specific, coupled CNDPs to limited sub-sectors (tobacco) should be favored over the implementation of broad, sector-spanning top-ups. Support to particular regions or sub- sectors would best be addressed under Pillar 2 as part of general rural development of a specific region. Opportunities 5.14 Bulgaria’s geographic location gives special importance to road transport. Over 70 percent oft he population of 7.7 million lives in urban areas. The capital Sofia has about 15 percent of the total population. Other important towns (Plovdiv, Varna, Burgas, Ruse, Stara Zagora and Pleven) have another 15 percent. This spatial distribution of the population tends to increase the demand for transport, especially roads. Foreign trade has been expanding at a rapid rate and is now growing at close to 15 percent per year in dollar terms. As a result, freight transport measured in terms oft on-kms increased between 2000 and 2003 by an average 5.5 percent per year for national transport, and by 10.4 percent for international transport. Most of this increase was carried by road transport, which grew by 14.4 percent per year, while rail freight decreased by an average 1.6 percent per year. The market share for road transport has therefore increased to 55 percent ofn ational transport, and to about two thirds for all freight transported in Bulgaria, including international transport (Table 5.3). The dominance ofr oad transport is still below the EU15 average where modal shares are 85 percent for road transport and 15 percent for rail. The proportion of imports and exports handled by road has also increased in the past five years and is currently at about 15 percent for exports and 22 percent for exports measured in terms oft onnage. 5.17 In countries with levels ofv ehicle ownership similar to that of Bulgaria (about 270 cars per 1,000 people), the rate of growth of road traffic can be much higher than GDP (the elasticity of demand with respect to GDP is greater than one-sometimes as high as about 2.0 for car traffic52). STRATEGIC PRIORITIES FORT HE ROAD NETWORK Identification of Road Sector Investment Priorities 5.22 The government’s stated priorities for investments in the road sector include: (i) Expansion and upgrading ofm otonvays and class Ir oads along the European corridors; (ii) Expansion and upgrading ofc omplementary national priority corridors that connect to the European corridors; (iii) Improved cross-border links with neighboring countries; (iv) Improvement oft ransit through cities and towns (bypasses); and (v) Maintenance and rehabilitation of the existing national and regional roads. 5.23 Whether investments in road assets are financed from public funds or by the private sector, road users and other beneficiaries ultimately pay for the investment through user fees or taxes. Consequently, investments should only be made in assets with high economic return and high strategc value for providing efficient road transport. It is therefore necessary to rigorously set priorities on the basis of economic efficiency and strategic goals within an integrated framework for planning and budgeting. Investment programs will need to be constrained by realistic estimates of available financial resources, taking into account existing commitments for ongoing projects and for debt servicing. The recurrent expenditure implications oft he public investment program will need to be systematically considered and closely integrated within the budgeting process in order not to reduce the productivity of earlier road infrastructure investments. Bulgaria could also finance part ofi ts needs in road transport from domestic capital markets. 5 SO PPP financing: Where economically justified and financially feasible, private participation in Bulgaria’s road investment program should be considered. Public-private partnerships bring significant advantages, as they (i)p rovide access to incremental financing to resource-constraint governments; (ii) create efficiency gains due to economies of scale, improved risk allocation and improved quality of service; (iii)a llow for earlier implementation of infrastructure projects, as government expenditures can be phased over time rather than requiring significant upfront investments; and (iv) can be recorded off- balance sheet as long as the construction risk and either the availability or demand risk is shifted to the private sector (EuroStat guidelines). PPPs should only be entered into if they provide value for money. This should be evaluated using the framework of a public sector comparator. In general, PPPs provide value as long as efficiency gains outweigh increased financing costs and risks retained by the government. Adequate risk sharing is therefore paramount to avoid unnecessary burdens on the government budget. In addition, PPPs require a stable and transparent legal framework and competitive bidding to ensure value for money and avoid overspending by government. The Government has a choice of structuring PPPs in the road sector as toll roads, shadow tolls, or availability payment schemes. Toll roads require sufficient traffic to generate adequate financial returns for private sector participation, and a free parallel road which can create significant traffic diversion. In addition, EU regulations forbid the concurrent charging of direct tolls and vignettes particularly for heavy trucks (greater than 12 tomes). Given these risks and the potential need for considerable government support, toll roads may not be feasible for most roads in Bulgaria due to the relatively low traffic flows. The government should therefore consider alternative options. Shadow tolls avoid traffic diversion at the cost of fluctuating government support. Availability payments based on performance criteria have proven a successful model for PPPs in the road sector in other Eastern European countries such as Hungary. Availability payments also have the benefit of predictable government obligations, which would need to be recorded on the government’s balance sheet.

CONCLUSION 5.56 Road infrastructure assets were negatively affected by the sharp decline in public investments during the period 1998-2002. This led to severe backlogs in road asset maintenance and rehabilitation, which in turn has adversely affected the movement of goods and people in Bulgaria, and added extra costs to the Bulgarian economy. 5.57 To clear the maintenance and rehabilitation backlog and to bring existing infrastructure to EU technical and safety standards, Bulgaria would have to use all of its current 1.1 percent of GDP road budget envelope (about EUR 250) on priority interventions with the highest economic returns, including maintenance programs, rehabilitation, upgrading and improvement of critical links as well as bypasses and bridges. 5.58 EU grants for the road sector are estimated to be about 0.5 percent of GDP per year, and it is suggested that these funds should be used for interventions that meet the economic return criterion, and are critical for economic growth and EU accession. Available data on traffic and construction costs suggest that rehabilitation and improvement of Class I roads on European corridors would yield the highest economic returns. Previous economic analyses have indicated that the Trakia and Struma proposed motonvay projects would have the required minimum economic rate of return. However, the estimated construction cost of these two motonvays is close to twice the estimated amount of EU cohesion grants expected to be made available to Bulgaria’s road sector over the period 2007-2013. CONCLUSIONS 6.23 The meeting of the environmental part of the acquis communautaire will increase demands on budgetary resources in Bulgaria over the next decade, and total spending on environmental protection is expected to increase by about 50 percent in 2004-2008 (while environment related capital expenditures are expected to increase three-fold, the current expenditures are expected to decline). Introduction Private decisions in finance confront tradeoffs, most notably that of risk and return. Policy decision making in the area of financial development is faced with similar tradeoffs, notably that between financial development and financial stability.1 However, not only tradeoffs exist in financial policy making. While prudential limits exist in extending access to credit, because not everyone is creditworthy or can handle credit responsibly—as we have learned most recently from the global financial crisis—a prudential limit may not exist for advancing access to deposits or insurance (Cull et al., 2012). Hence, synergies can also be found and exploited. Financial policy reforms may thus focus on synergies first, i.e. advancing financial development and improving financial sector resilience at the same time. We study one such possible synergy in this paper; namely, the positive effect that greater financial inclusion in deposits can have on greater reliability of bank deposit funding in times of stress. From 2006 to 2009, growth of bank deposits dropped by over 12 percentage points globally. The most affected by the 2008 global crisis were upper middle income countries that experienced a drop of 15 percentage points on average. Individual countries such as Azerbaijan, Botswana, Iceland, and Montenegro switched from deposit growth of 58 percent, 31 percent, 57 percent, and 94 percent in 2007 to deposit declines (or a complete stop in deposit growth) of -2 percent, 1 percent, -1 percent, -8 percent in 2009, respectively. In times of financial stress or crises, depositors get anxious, can run on banks, and withdraw their deposits (Diamond and Dybvig, 1983; Shin, 2009). Large depositors are usually the first ones to run (Huang and Ratnovski, 2011). By the law of large numbers, correlated deposit withdrawals could be mitigated if bank deposits are more diversified. Greater diversification of deposits could be achieved by enabling a broader access to and use of bank deposits, i.e. involving a greater share of adult population in the use of bank deposits (financial inclusion). Based on this assumption, broader financial inclusion in

be mitigated if bank deposits are more diversified. Greater diversification of deposits could be achieved by enabling a broader access to and use of bank deposits, i.e. involving a greater share of adult population in the use of bank deposits (financial inclusion). Based on this assumption, broader financial inclusion in bank deposits could significantly improve resilience of banking sector funding and thus overall financial stability (Cull et al., 2012). This paper investigates the implications of a broader access to deposits for the dynamics of bank deposits during the global financial crisis. Namely, we analyze whether access to bank deposits by a larger share of a country’s population can help explain differences in the drop of deposit growth over 2007-2010 across our sample of 95 countries. We also separately estimate the differences in the relationship between the drop in deposit growth and access to deposits for low-income (LIC), middle-income (MIC), and high-income (HIC) countries. Moreover, we use robust regressions to gauge the impact of outliers on the estimation results. While this finding holds for the entire sample of HICs, MICs, and LICs, it could be particularly strong in MICs, where a large share of population still lacks access to bank deposits, trust in banks is yet to be firmly established, and the integration in global financial flows is growing. In addition to the access and use of deposits, bank stability—measured by the aggregate z-score, and the dummy for the occurrence of banking crises are the most significant explanatory variables in our regressions. The results hold even when accounting for the possible leverage effects of outliers. The main message is that countries should recognize that policies to promote a broader use of bank deposits could improve resilience of bank funding. Such policies can thus enhance overall financial stability and complement the mainstream macroprudential policies to foster stability of the financial system. Our paper responds to an existing gap in the empirical literature linking greater access to deposits with greater financial (banking sector) stability. While the literature postulates that an inclusive financial sector will have a more diversified, stable retail deposit base that can increase systemic stability, empirical research confirming existence of such a relationship, especially at the level of the financial system, is largely absent in the literature (GPFI, 2012; Cull et al., 2012; Prasad, 2010). At the individual and household level, savings support stability and, given their very large numbers, small savers potentially contribute to stability at the financial system level (Cull et al., 2012). Low income savers tend to maintain steady financial behavior through the business cycle. Hence, during crises, deposits from low income clients typically act as a continued source of funds even when other sources of bank financing dry up or become difficult to roll over. Small customers thus provide big opportunities to mobilize stable deposits (Khan, 2011). Greater financial inclusion, including access to savings, can also enhance financial stability indirectly, by providing individuals, households, and small firms with greater access to financial risk-managing tools. This greater access can enhance resilience and stability of the real economy and thus also the financial system that serves it (GPFI, 2012; Cull et al., 2012; Khan, 2011). At the bank level, focusing on retail deposit generation can produce a more diversified and stable funding base that is less sensitive to changes in market interest rates and a bank’s financial condition. At the bank level, focusing on retail deposit generation can produce a more diversified and stable funding base that is less sensitive to changes in market interest rates and a bank’s financial condition. In stress times, insured depositors have proven to be a bank’s most reliable funding source and, therefore, play an integral role in mitigating liquidity risk (OCC, 2012). The global crisis demonstrated that stable retail sources of funding, in contrast with reliance on borrowed funds, can greatly enhance the soundness and resilience of financial institutions and reduce volatility of earnings (Khan, 2011). Diversified funding base of financial institutions has played a role in cushioning the impact of a global credit (wholesale funding) crunch on domestic financial intermediation (Hannig and Jansen, 2010). At the country level, financial inclusion can boost efficiency of financial intermediation, through intermediation of greater amounts of domestic savings, and thus improve soundness of investment financing and investment cycles. Provided that quality financial infrastructure and competent supervision are implemented, such improvement will, in turn, produce both greater economic and financial stability (Prasad, 2010; Cull et al., 2012). Similarly, banking sectors with a stronger liquidity position have a large capacity to meet deposit withdrawal demand of a given size, and should thus be more credible and less prone to deposit withdrawals. More concentrated banking systems could be more prone to deposit withdrawals due to possibly greater interconnectedness and thus greater worries of depositors about transmission of problems from one bank to another and subsequently to the whole system. Banking systems with higher levels of deposits per GDP are susceptible, centeris paribus, to greater deposit withdrawals simply because they have greater risk exposure in the regard. Banks with greater loan to deposit ratios can be considered, from the view point of depositors, better monitored and safer than banks with very low loan to deposit ratios because of the covenants and the resulting external monitoring that credit financing of banks entails. Note that the financing position of banks with high loan to deposit ratios can still be more vulnerable overall, as informed creditors are typically the first to run. However, here we analyze the reliability (stickiness) of bank deposit funding not the entire financing of the bank. Finally, countries with greater capital account openness are more integrated in global finance which can protect them against (diversify away) domestic shocks, but also exposes them to foreign shocks, including negative spillovers of crises in the region or capital sending countries. We handle the possible endogeneity of explanatory variables by dating most of them prior to the crisis and running an ordinary least square (OLS) regression with robust standard errors. In addition, we test the robustness of our baseline results to outliers by running robust regression estimation that proportionally underweights the information from leverage points (outliners) in the regression estimation. Further, since our alternative measure of access to deposits based on Demirguc-Kunt and Klapper (2012) is dated by 2011, and because GDP growth could also suffer an endogeneity problem, we estimate the regression model by GMM in addition. In this case, we use the Honohan (2008) index based on data from 2005 as an instrument for the 2011 Demirguc-Kunt and Klapper’s index, and the log of GDP at the peak of deposit growth prior to the crisis as an instrument for GDP growth during the period when the maximum drop of deposit growth occurred in each country. We have used the rule of thumb of Stock, Wright and Yogo (2002) and Stock and Yogo (2005) to check that our instruments are relevant and our GMM regression does not suffer from the weak instrument problem. 4. We thus focus on analyzing the dynamics of bank deposit growth between 2006-2010, which covers both pre-crisis years and post-crisis years. We calculate year on year growth rate on bank deposits for 173 countries using data on outstanding deposits of commercial banks from IMF’s Financial Access Survey (FAS) database. We choose this indicator over other measures of total deposits to ensure

We calculate year on year growth rate on bank deposits for 173 countries using data on outstanding deposits of commercial banks from IMF’s Financial Access Survey (FAS) database. We choose this indicator over other measures of total deposits to ensure maximum cross sectional coverage (number of countries covered) and best consistency across countries. We observed that it is rarely the case that the year on year deposit growth rate remained stable and many countries experienced more than one peak or more than one trough during the period that we examine. In order to capture the potential impact of the 2008 crisis, we define maximum drop in deposit growth in the following manner: first, we document the minimum deposit growth a country experienced between 2007 and 2010 and mark the year when it occurred; then we find the maximum deposit growth the country had experienced before this year. The difference between this maximum deposit growth and the minimum deposit growth then constitutes the maximum drop in deposit growth—our cross-country dependent variable. We use the composite indicator of access to financial services constructed by Honohan (2008) as a proxy for access to deposits. The actual use of deposits in each country is approximated by the indicator “percentage of adult population who saved at a formal financial institution in the past year” from the Global Financial Inclusion Database (Demirguc-Kunt and Klapper (2012)).2 Detailed descriptions of variables, data sources, and data availability are listed in Table A1. 2 Earlier attempts at measuring access to bank deposits include Beck, Demirguc-Kunt, and Martinez Peria (2007). We do not use this measure as it is available for a much smaller number of countries and because it is highly correlated with deposits over GDP, which we use as a control, and that would introduce a serious multi-colinearity problem. We use indicators of growth in aggregate output, income per capita, inflation, and population to control for the economic growth during the global crisis period, for the difference in economic development, for the change in price level, and for the difference in the country size. Our hypothesis is that middle-income countries could benefit from a greater synergy between improving access to deposits together with improvements in banking sector stability (the deposit funding base of banks); that is financial inclusion and stability going in the same direction. This is because LICs face huge financial inclusion gaps and can mobilize much less savings from households that are often consumption-constrained. Moreover, LICs are not as well integrated in global finance to import large amounts of foreign savings, and to be subject to cross-border shocks, including those to depositor confidence. In contrast, access to bank deposits in high-income countries approaches 90–100 percent, and high- income countries focus mainly on fostering financial stability, with only marginal gains from further improving access to deposits. We thus investigate the relationship between access to deposits and bank funding stability separately for countries in different income groups next. 6. Namely, external and whole sale funding has a number of covenants, notably prudential ones, to which a bank needs to adhere to secure and roll over such funding. This result could arise because banks in LIsub countries have typically large z-scores and capital buffers, to the extent that the buffers can be judged inefficient. In turn, the cross-country variation in z-scores may not necessarily reflect a banking sector’s concern about hedging unexpected losses. In addition, the leeway of banks to smooth profits, for instance because of different provisioning rules or accounting standards that tend to be looser in LICs, could further blur the role of z-scores in measuring the ability of banks to absorb unexpected losses. In sum, this section established that the positive influence of greater access to and the use of deposits on the stability of bank deposit growth (and thus stability of bank deposit funding) during the 2008 global financial crisis is stronger in MICs compared with HICs and with LICs. In LICs this positive influence may not be significant. For HICs and LICs, further research on bigger data samples is needed to obtain more reliable inference. 7. Conclusion This paper examined the effect of access to bank deposits on the stability of deposit growth during the 2008 global financial crisis using a cross-sectional regression model for 95 countries. It found that, on average, greater access to bank deposits or their actual use by a country’s population can enhance resilience of the deposit funding base of the banking sector in times of financial stress. Specifically, the estimated coefficient on the variables measuring access to deposits indicate that a 10 percent increase in the share of people that have access to bank deposits can mitigate the deposit growth drops (or deposit withdrawal rates) by about three to eight percentage points. The enhanced resilience of bank funding can then support overall financial stability of the banking sector and the entire financial system. We also found that this effect is likely much stronger in middle-income countries, which could face greater shocks to depositor confidence due to still developing trust in the banking sector and already high integration in global finance. is likely much stronger in middle-income countries, which could face greater shocks to depositor confidence due to still developing trust in the banking sector and already high integration in global finance. For high-income and low-income countries more research is needed to obtain more reliable conclusions with the help of bigger or richer datasets. Our findings have important policy implications. Policy makers face tradeoffs when deciding whether to focus on reforms to promote financial development (financial inclusion, innovation, competition, etc.) or whether to focus on further improvements in financial stability (microprudential, macroprudential, business conduct supervision, etc.). However, synergies between promoting financial development and financial stability can also exist as shown in this paper. We recommend that policy makers focus first on taking advantage of such synergies in their framework for financial sector policy. This framework is typically formulated in a national financial sector strategy which sets the development goals in finance, in view of systemic risk associated with achieving these goals and the risk preference of the country government. Namely, we argue that involving more people in the use of bank deposits could be beneficial for people, economic development, and stability of the financial system alike. Countries should strive to promote a broader use of bank deposits not only to aid economic development and poverty alleviation but also to complement the mainstream macroprudential policies to enhance financial stability. Again, these policy efforts, their synergetic effects, and the plan for their implementation, including the resulting responsibilities of different government agencies, should be clearly described in the national financial sector strategy. With proper regulation and oversight in place, initiatives such as Kenya’s M-PESA and M-KESHO projects (Demombynes and Thegeya, 2012) or South Africa’s Mzansi accounts (Bankable Frontier Associates, 2009) could serve as good examples of promoting a broader use of bank accounts (deposits) and enhancing the reliability of bank deposit funding at the same time. Our analysis is subject to some caveats that could be addressed in future research. An important mitigating factor of deposit withdrawals that addresses the informational asymmetry between banks and depositors is microprudential supervision. We have considered a proxy of the quality of microprudential supervision following (Anginer, Demirguc-Kunt, and Zhu, 2012) in our baseline estimation. But including this variable reduced our sample by one third and the variable was not significant. A better proxy of microprudential supervision available for more countries could be employed in future research. Further, we have not explicitly modeled the negative confidence shocks from crises in the adjacent region or similar countries, even though we have controlled for capital account openness. Finally, the wave of crises after 2008 triggered various policy responses, including injections of public capital in banks, increases in the limits for public deposit insurance, and blanket deposit guarantees. The data on relevant policy interventions are not readily available for a sufficient number of countries to our knowledge. The data could be collected as part of future research to control for relevant policy responses, many of which have been endogenous to deposit growth and will have to be appropriately instrumented. the Bank, the associated expected specific results and the Bank’s appraisal of the program; s. Supplemental DPF Document: means a document that provides the information required under paragraph 32 of this policy. SECTION III – SCOPE 4. The Bank provides DPF in the form of a policy-based Bank Loan or a policy-based Bank Guarantee. A DPF is aimed at helping a Member Country address actual or anticipated development financing requirements that have domestic or external origins. The Bank may provide a Bank Loan to a Member Country or to one of its Political Subdivisions; and it may provide a Bank Guarantee of debt incurred by a Member Country or by one of its Political Subdivisions.1 5. If a Bank Loan is made to a Political Subdivision of a Member Country: (a) the Political Subdivision is required to have the legal authority necessary to borrow directly from, and enter into an agreement with, the Bank; and (b) the Member Country provides the Bank with a Member Country Guarantee. A Bank Guarantee provided to guarantee the debt of a Political Subdivision requires a Member Country Indemnity. If a Bank Loan is made to a Political Subdivision or a Bank Guarantee is made to guarantee the debt of a Political Subdivision, the considerations and requirements applicable to the Member Country set out in this Policy apply equally to the Political Subdivision, as relevant. Considerations for Development Policy Operations 6. General: Through development policy operations, the Bank supports a Member Country’s program of policy and institutional actions that promote growth and sustainable poverty reduction. Development policy operations are supportive of, and consistent with, the Member Country’s economic and sectoral policies and institutions aimed at broad-based sustainable growth and efficient resource allocation. They support a program of policy and institutional actions, for example, to improve the investment climate, diversify the economy, create employment, improve public finances, strengthen service delivery, and meet applicable international commitments. Any Investment Project Financing or Program-for- Results Financing subcomponent included in a DPF is subject to the relevant operational policies for Investment Project Financing and Program-for-Results Financing, respectively. 1 See Policy: Lending Operations: Choice of Borrower and contractual agreements. 7. Financing Criteria and Selectivity: The Bank’s decision to extend a DPF is based on an assessment of the Member Country’s policy and institutional framework—including its economic situation, governance, environmental/natural resource management, and poverty and social aspects. The Bank considers the strength of the program proposed for support and the Member Country’s commitment to, and ownership of, the program against its track record. It also assesses the Member Country’s institutional capacity and ability to effectively implement the program to be supported and describes the country’s capacity- building efforts. 8. Macroeconomic Framework: The Bank provides a DPF for a Member Country or its Political Subdivision only when it has determined that the Member Country’s macroeconomic policy framework is adequate.2 If the DPF is made as a Bank Guarantee of debt of an IDA Member Country or its Political Subdivision, the Member Country must also have low or moderate risk of debt distress and comply with

only when it has determined that the Member Country’s macroeconomic policy framework is adequate.2 If the DPF is made as a Bank Guarantee of debt of an IDA Member Country or its Political Subdivision, the Member Country must also have low or moderate risk of debt distress and comply with applicable Bank policies relating to non- concessional borrowing. In addition, if the DPF is a Bank Loan to a Political Subdivision or a Bank Guarantee guaranteeing the debt of a Political Subdivision, the Political Subdivision has an adequate expenditure program, sustainable debt, and adequate fiscal arrangements with the central government in accordance with the country’s constitutional and legislative framework. 9. Consultations and Participation: In carrying out dialogue with a Member Country, the Bank advises it to consult with and engage the participation of key stakeholders in the country in the process of formulating its development strategies. Key stakeholders include social groups directly affected by the operations, as well as public sector, private sector, and donor organizations relevant to the operation. For a development policy operation, the Member Country draws on this process of strategy formulation to determine, in the context of its constitutional and legislative framework, the form and extent of consultations and participation in preparing, implementing, and monitoring and evaluating the operation. The Bank’s Program Document (PD) describes the Member Country’s arrangements for consultations and participation relevant to the operation, and the outcomes of the participatory process adopted in formulating the Member Country’s development strategy. Relevant analytic work conducted by the Bank, particularly on poverty and social impacts and on environmental aspects, is made available to the public as part of the consultation process, in accordance with the Bank’s Policy on Access to Information. 10.Coordination with Development Partners: In preparing development policy operations, the Bank collaborates with the IMF and other international financing institutions and donors, as appropriate, while retaining responsibility for its financing decisions. Design of Development Policy Operations 11.Development Objectives: The Executive Directors consider and approve each DPF as meeting the special circumstances provision of the Bank’s Articles of Agreement. The program design includes measurable indicators for monitoring and evaluating the results on completion. 12.Analytic Underpinnings: A development policy operation draws on relevant analytic work on the Member Country undertaken by the Bank, the Member Country, and third parties, for example, as appropriate, analyses of the Member Country’s economy wide or sectoral policies and institutions aimed at stimulating investment, creating employment, and accelerating and sustaining growth, as well as analyses of the poverty and social impacts of proposed policies,4 environment and natural resource management, governance and public expenditure management, procurement, and financial accountability systems. The Program Document describes the main pieces of analytic work used in the preparation of the operation and shows how they are linked to the proposed development policy program. 13.Poverty and Social Impacts: The Bank determines whether specific policies supported by the operation are likely to have significant poverty and social consequences, especially on poor people and vulnerable groups. For policies with likely significant effects, the Bank summarizes in the Program Document relevant analytic knowledge of these effects and of the Member Country’s systems for reducing adverse effects and enhancing positive effects associated with the specific policies being supported. If there are significant gaps in the analysis or shortcomings in these systems, the Bank describes in the Program Document how such gaps or shortcomings would be addressed before or during program implementation, as appropriate. 14.Environmental, Forests, and other Natural Resource Aspects: The Bank determines whether specific country policies supported by the operation are likely to cause significant effects on the Member Country’s environment, forests, and other natural resources. For policies with likely significant effects, the Bank assesses in the Program Document the Member Country’s systems for reducing such adverse effects and enhancing positive effects, drawing on relevant country-level or sectoral environmental analysis. If there are significant gaps in the analysis or shortcomings in these systems, the Bank describes in the Program Document how such gaps or shortcomings would be addressed before or during program implementation, as appropriate. 15.Program Funding and Size of Operation: The Bank extends a DPF only when the overall program is adequately funded, considering both domestic and external sources of finance. The size of each DPF is determined individually on the basis of the Member Country’s circumstances, including the overall projected financing requirements at the time of the operation, the availability of alternative financing, debt sustainability, creditworthiness and IBRD exposure (for IBRD borrowers) or relative claim on available concessional resources (for IDA countries). Bank approval of the DPF is subject to maintenance of an adequate macroeconomic policy framework, implementation of the overall program in a manner satisfactory to the Bank, and compliance with the program’s prior actions. Disbursement under a Bank Loan5, and signing of each agreement providing for a Bank Guarantee, is conditioned on: (a) satisfactory implementation of the program supported by the DPF, including compliance with the program’s prior actions and tranche release conditions (in the case of a multi-tranche Bank Loan); and (b) maintenance of a satisfactory macroeconomic policy framework. The Bank seeks to harmonize these conditions with those of other development partners in consultation with the Member Country. 17.Operational Structure: All development policy operations are embedded in an explicit medium-term framework and are based on adequate prior policy and institutional actions. DPF in the form of a Bank Loan may be provided in one or more tranches, depending on the Member Country’s policy environment and capacity, its financing requirements and other available financing, and the content and phasing of the program being supported by the development policy operation. Development policy operations following a programmatic approach consist of a series of operations within a medium-term framework of policy and institutional actions. Such programmatic approach involves (a) clear, monitorable indicators with quantitative baselines and targets, whenever possible, (b) indicative prior actions (or triggers) for the subsequent operations in the series, and (c) notional timing and amounts of subsequent operations. 18.Bank Guarantees: A Bank Guarantee covers a Member Country’s (or its Political Subdivision’s) debt service defaults. The Bank only provides guarantees to the extent necessary to mobilize private financing, taking into account country and market circumstances. The Member Country requesting the Bank Guarantee provides a Member Country Indemnity to the Bank. The indemnity is provided by the Member Country, not its Political Subdivision, even if the debt guaranteed is that of the Political Subdivision. If the Bank Guarantee is funded under a trust fund, and the constituent documents of the trust fund permit, the Bank may forego the requirement of a Member Country Indemnity. The portion of debt guaranteed by the Bank is not subject to debt rescheduling or debt restructuring without the Bank’s consent. 19.Risk Management: The Member Country is responsible for managing operational risks affecting the development effectiveness of the development policy operation.
